name: Tesamorelin (off-label)
class: GHRH analog used outside its approved indication
evidenceNote: Outside HIV, two randomized, placebo-controlled trials exist: 60 adults with abdominal obesity and 152 older adults tested for cognition. They are small and short next to the HIV program that won approval, and none tested anti-aging or muscle building.
summary: Tesamorelin is FDA-approved only for belly fat in HIV lipodystrophy. Wellness use for fat loss or aging rests on small trials.
keyTakeaway: Tesamorelin is a 44-amino-acid analog of growth hormone releasing hormone, approved by the FDA since 2010 as Egrifta to reduce excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV lipodystrophy. Wellness clinics also use it off-label for body composition and aging. Outside HIV, a 12-month trial in 60 obese adults cut visceral fat versus placebo, and a 20-week trial in older adults found modest cognitive gains. Because tesamorelin is licensed as a biological product, FDA rules leave no lawful path for compounded copies. It is banned in sport.

blocks.text: Tesamorelin is a synthetic version of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH), the brain signal that tells the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. It is a chain of 44 amino acids [1]. The approved drug, Egrifta, is made by Theratechnologies and is indicated only to reduce excess abdominal fat in adults with HIV who have lipodystrophy, an abnormal redistribution of body fat linked to HIV treatment [1].

This entry covers its use for other purposes: shrinking visceral fat, the fat packed around the organs, in people without HIV, and general body-composition or anti-aging goals. Prescribing an approved drug for an unapproved purpose is called off-label use. The approved product has its own entry in the library.

Tesamorelin binds GHRH receptors in the pituitary and prompts the gland to release more of its own growth hormone. That in turn raises IGF-1 and its binding protein IGFBP-3, the main messengers of growth hormone's effects in tissues [1]. The label describes growth hormone as having both anabolic (tissue-building) and lipolytic (fat-breaking) actions [1].
Its signature effect in trials is a selective drop in visceral fat with little change in the fat under the skin of the belly or limbs [3][5].

No. Tesamorelin itself has been FDA-approved since 2010, but only for one use. The label also states that it is not indicated for weight loss, that its long-term cardiovascular safety has not been established, and that it must not be used in pregnancy, with active cancer, or with a disrupted hypothalamic-pituitary axis [1].

Two versions are marketed, Egrifta SV and Egrifta WR. The WR form, labeled in March 2025, is an 11.6 mg vial that is mixed once and supplies daily doses for a week, and its label states that the two products differ in dose, mixing, and storage and are not interchangeable [2]. A doctor may legally prescribe either off-label, but no regulator has reviewed evidence for those uses.

The HIV evidence is solid. Among 404 randomized participants with HIV and excess belly fat, visceral fat fell 10.9% over six months on tesamorelin versus 0.6% on placebo, IGF-1 rose, and glucose measures did not change [3]. In an extension, the reduction held at about 18% through 52 weeks, but fat came back in people switched to placebo [4].
Off-label use rests on a much smaller set of trials:

rows: 60 abdominally obese adults without HIV with low growth hormone output; 12 months vs placebo
Visceral fat fell (treatment effect of 35 cm2), with lower triglycerides, CRP, and carotid wall thickness; no change in glucose [5]
152 adults aged 55 to 87, healthy or with mild cognitive impairment; 20 weeks vs placebo
Small improvement in executive function; body fat down 7.4%; IGF-1 up 117%; mild adverse events in 68% vs 36% on placebo [6]

blocks.text: These trials are encouraging for specific measures but do not test what wellness clinics often promise. The obesity trial enrolled people selected for low growth hormone secretion, and the cognition trial was short. Neither looked at muscle strength, longevity, or skin, and the HIV data show that the fat effect disappears once injections stop [4].

Side effects seen with the approved drug apply to any use. In the pooled 26-week HIV trials, injection site reactions occurred in 17% on tesamorelin versus 6% on placebo, and joint pain, muscle pain, and swelling in the limbs were also common [1]. The label warns about raised IGF-1, fluid retention, glucose intolerance, and allergic reactions [1].

Not lawfully, under current FDA policy. Tesamorelin is licensed as a biological product, under BLA 022505 [1], and the FDA states that biological products are not eligible for the exemptions that let 503A pharmacies and 503B outsourcing facilities compound drugs [7]. Compounded drugs in general are not FDA-approved, so their safety, strength, and quality are not checked before sale [7].

A 2026 clinical review lists tesamorelin among growth hormone axis peptides that turn up in online self-administration protocols, where product composition, dose, and stacking with other compounds are uncertain [9]. In competitive sport, the World Anti-Doping Agency's 2026 list names tesamorelin as a prohibited GHRH analog [8].
